title: Sacraments as instruments (ST III.62)
hookLine: God uses sacraments like a craftsman uses tools

lines: A VIOLIN IN ITS CASE IS SILENT.
cards: A violin lying in its case makes no music. Put it in a player's hands and the room is full. So who made the music?
The player, obviously. And yet it's not the player's voice you're hearing. It's the violin's, with the grain of that wood in it.
Back on day one hundred twenty-five, a sacrament was a sign that does something. Thomas asks who is really doing it, through water, oil, bread, words. His answer turns on a craftsman and a tool.

teach.h: A PRINCIPAL CAUSE AND AN INSTRUMENT.
teach.b: Thomas sorts causes into two kinds. A principal cause works by its own power, the way fire heats. An instrumental cause works because something greater moves it.
His picture is a carpenter and an axe. The bed looks like the plan in the carpenter's head, not like the axe. But the carpenter really works through it.
So, Thomas says, God is the principal cause of grace, and the sacraments are his instruments. Baptism's water doesn't hold grace like a jar holds coins.
God gives grace through it, the way the carpenter cuts through the axe. Then a detail that makes this more than a metaphor. An instrument has its own action too.

teach.h: THE AXE CUTS BECAUSE IT'S SHARP.
teach.b: The axe cuts because it's sharp; that's exactly how it serves the carpenter. In the same way, water washes. Bread feeds.
Oil soothes. The sign isn't arbitrary: the sacrament's own action is the shape God's work takes.

That's why Paul, in the Douay-Rheims, can speak of being saved "by the laver of regeneration, and renovation of the Holy Ghost." A laver is a washing basin. The washing is the instrument; the new life is God's.
One more step. Thomas calls Christ's own humanity an instrument joined to God, like a hand.

teach.h: A HAND, AND A TOOL IN THE HAND.
teach.b: The sacraments are instruments set apart, like a tool that hand picks up.

So grace flows from God, through Christ, through the sacrament, to a person. Christians understand sacraments in different ways; some churches see baptism and the Lord's Supper mainly as signs and acts of obedience.
Thomas's picture is that God really works through the tool.

how: Catholics receive the sacraments as signs through which Christ gives grace, and the Church teaches that they work by the action of Christ himself, not by the holiness of the minister.

o: yes, the water itself is the source.
God gives grace through it, as a carpenter through an axe.
no, the water does nothing at all.
games.why: God is the principal cause; the sacrament is his instrument, and its own action, washing, is how it serves.

practice: Pick up one ordinary tool within reach, a pen, a cup, a spoon, a key, and feel its weight, its edges, what it's made for.
Use it once, deliberately, noticing how it does what it does, the pen by its ink, the cup by its shape, then set it down gently, as if it mattered. If you pray, ask to be a good tool in God's hands.

wordCard.voice: Sacraments as instruments. For Thomas, God is the principal cause of grace, and the sacraments are his tools, working by their own action, washing, feeding, anointing. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: a tool, something used to get work done.
